reason: The sources provide over a dozen cross-verified claims across four independent sites detailing Galileo's historic 1991 flyby of asteroid 951 Gaspra.
story: On October 29, 1991, NASA's Galileo spacecraft made history on its journey to Jupiter by making humanity's first close flyby of an asteroid: 951 Gaspra. Discovered by astronomer G. N. Neujmin in 1916, Gaspra had only ever been seen as a point of light in telescopes. Because its precise position in space was uncertain by hundreds of kilometers, Galileo's team relied on an innovative optical navigation campaign using approach images to lock onto the asteroid. Flying past at high speed, Galileo captured 57 images, snapping its closest views from 5,300 kilometers away. The photos revealed an irregular, heavily faceted body lacking large craters comparable to its radius, confirming Gaspra formed relatively recently from the catastrophic breakup of a parent asteroid. Galileo also revealed prominent surface grooves up to 300 meters wide—fracture features previously seen only on Mars's moon Phobos.
angle: When Galileo completed humanity's first-ever asteroid flyby in 1991, it revealed mysterious fracture grooves across Gaspra that had previously only been seen on the Martian moon Phobos.

claims.claim: The Galileo spacecraft flew past asteroid 951 Gaspra on October 29, 1991.
Gaspra was visited while the Galileo spacecraft was en route to explore Jupiter.
Asteroid 951 Gaspra was discovered in 1916 by astronomer G. N. Neujmin.
Gaspra completes one orbit around the Sun in 3.29 years.
Gaspra orbits the Sun at an average distance of approximately 2.21 astronomical units.
Galileo captured its closest images of Gaspra from a distance of 5,300 kilometers (3,300 miles).
The highest image resolution achieved during the Gaspra flyby was approximately 54 meters per pixel.
Gaspra rotates with a period of roughly 7 hours (approximately 0.293 days).
Fifty-seven images were returned or produced from the Galileo flyby encounter with Gaspra.
Gaspra's surface lacks large impact craters comparable in size to the asteroid's radius.
Gaspra has linear groove-like depressions that are 100 to 300 meters wide and tens of meters deep.
Grooves like those discovered on Gaspra had previously only been observed on Mars's moon Phobos.
Gaspra's morphology is consistent with an origin resulting from the collisional breakup of a larger parent asteroid.
Following its encounter with Gaspra, Galileo was targeted to fly past asteroid 243 Ida.

disputed: Dimensions of Gaspra: S2 describes it in one place as roughly 17 km long by 10 km wide, and in another place as approximately 19 x 12 x 11 km. A script should cite its irregular dimensions generally or qualify specific measurements with 'approximately'.

Origin of flat facets and concavities: S1 notes it is uncertain whether large flat areas like Dunne Regio are impact craters distorted by weak gravity or break-off facets created when Gaspra separated from its parent body. A script should present both possibilities as competing hypotheses.

Presence and thickness of regolith: S1 highlights ongoing scientific debate over whether Gaspra retains a significant regolith layer given its very low escape velocity, whereas visual features suggest a mantled surface. A script should frame the presence of regolith as a debated scientific puzzle.
